title: Fifty-four years, 33 moments
lede: From a bar in Sunnyvale to a landfill in New Mexico, and through every later owner of the name. Filter by thread.

events.title: Atari founded; Pong
events.text: Nolan Bushnell founds Atari. Engineer Al Alcorn builds Pong, which is tested in bars in Grass Valley and Sunnyvale, California.

events.title: Home Pong
events.text: A home version of Pong is sold through Sears, which a reference history says agreed to buy all 100,000 units.

events.title: Warner buys Atari for $28 million
events.text: Warner Communications acquires the company from Bushnell, mainly at the urging of executive Emanuel Gerard.

events.title: The Video Computer System
events.text: Atari launches the cartridge-based VCS, later renamed the 2600.

events.title: Kassar replaces Bushnell
events.text: Warner removes Bushnell and installs Raymond Kassar, from Burlington Industries. Revenue for 1978 is under $200 million.

events.title: The programmers walk out
events.text: Four game programmers leave after being refused credit and royalties, and found Activision.

events.title: First third-party cartridges
events.text: Activision ships Fishing Derby, Dragster and Boxing for the Atari console.

events.title: Revenue passes $415 million
events.text: A reference history puts Atari’s 1980 revenue above $415 million, more than double the year before.

events.title: Distributors asked to commit for a year
events.text: Atari asks distributors to place orders for virtually all of 1982. It has about 80 percent of the market.

events.title: Pac-Man for the 2600
events.text: The cartridge is criticised for its graphics and sells well. Atari expected to sell nine million, according to a reference history.

events.title: The peak year
events.text: Sales of about $2 billion, operating profit of $323 million and 10,000 employees.

events.title: The earnings warning
events.text: Warner says fourth-quarter earnings will be about 60 cents a share against expectations of $1.60 to $2.00. The stock falls $16.75 the next trading day.

events.title: Insider sales disclosed
events.text: Warner chairman Steven Ross discloses that Kassar sold 5,000 shares on December 8 and another executive sold 6,376 on December 1. The stock closes at $29.50.

events.title: Manufacturing moves to Asia
events.text: Atari moves production to Hong Kong and Taiwan, eliminating 1,700 U.S. jobs.

events.title: First operating loss
events.text: Atari loses $45.6 million, against a profit of $100.6 million a year earlier.

events.title: Kassar resigns
events.text: James J. Morgan of Philip Morris is named to succeed him from September 6.

events.title: The Alamogordo burial
events.text: Fourteen truckloads of cartridges and equipment are dumped in a New Mexico landfill and covered in concrete. Atari’s second-quarter loss was $310.5 million.

events.title: $536 million lost in nine months
events.text: Atari reports a third-quarter loss of about $180 million. Mattel’s electronics division has lost $201 million so far in the year.

events.title: Warner under siege
events.text: Rupert Murdoch seeks up to 49.9 percent of Warner, whose shares have traded as low as $19.

events.title: Sold to Jack Tramiel
events.text: Warner sells the home computer and video game business for $240 million in notes and no cash, keeps the coin-operated division and takes a $425 million loss.

events.title: The 2600 returns at $40
events.text: Atari Corporation relaunches the console as Nintendo and Sega enter the U.S. market. More than 20 million have been sold.

events.title: The Jaguar
events.text: Atari Corporation introduces a 64-bit console at $249.99.

events.title: The Jaguar fails
events.text: About 125,000 units sold since launch, 100,000 unsold in inventory, and a net loss of $49.6 million on revenue of $14.6 million.

events.title: Merger with a disk-drive maker
events.text: Atari Corporation agrees to merge into JTS in a stock swap worth about $75 million. The merger closes in July.

events.title: Hasbro buys the name for $5 million
events.text: JTS sells the Atari games, trademarks and licences to a subsidiary of Hasbro Interactive.

events.title: Infogrames buys Hasbro Interactive
events.text: The French publisher pays $100 million for the division, which includes the Atari properties.

events.title: Infogrames becomes Atari
events.text: Infogrames, Inc. changes its name to Atari, Inc. Its Nasdaq symbol becomes ATAR.

events.title: The parent buys out the U.S. company
events.text: Infogrames Entertainment agrees to pay $1.68 a share for the 49 percent of Atari, Inc. it does not own.

events.title: Chapter 11
events.text: Atari Inc., Atari Interactive and two affiliates file in the Southern District of New York to separate from the French parent, by then called Atari S.A.

events.title: Bankruptcy plan approved
events.text: The court approves a plan that pays unsecured creditors, owed a reported $10.3 million, about $1.75 million over three years.

events.title: The dig
events.text: A documentary crew excavates the Alamogordo landfill and finds E.T. cartridges in front of about 200 onlookers.

events.title: Wade Rosen becomes chief executive
events.text: The chairman of Atari SA takes over from Frédéric Chesnais.

events.title: €56.0M of revenue
events.text: Atari SA reports its third straight year of growth and a small net profit, and moves its registered office to Luxembourg.
